_comment: Media definitions for popular, well-studied objects, displayed in the detail panel by js/render3d.js. Priority: (1) a real photograph where humanity has one (photo.kind='photo'), (2) an official NASA/ESO artist's impression (photo.kind='art'), (3) a procedural WebGL render generated from published parameters ('type') — also the automatic fallback if a photo fails to load. Photos are served from Wikimedia Commons via the stable Special:FilePath endpoint; 'file' is the exact Commons filename (verified via Commons search July 2026). Every media item is credited on screen. Star colors for procedural renders derive from params.tempK; planet palettes are artistic but consistent with true-color spacecraft imagery.

entries.title: Mercury
entries.blurb: The smallest planet and closest to the Sun — a cratered, airless world scorched to 430 °C by day and frozen at night.

entries.title: Venus
entries.blurb: Earth's hellish twin: a runaway greenhouse world hidden under unbroken sulfuric-acid clouds, hotter at the surface than Mercury.

entries.title: Mars
entries.blurb: The red planet — iron-oxide deserts, the Solar System's tallest volcano, and polar caps of water and CO₂ ice.

entries.title: Jupiter

photo.file: Jupiter and its shrunken Great Red Spot.jpg

entries.blurb: The largest planet, a gas giant with banded ammonia clouds and a centuries-old storm bigger than Earth.

entries.title: Saturn
entries.blurb: The ringed giant: its icy ring system spans 280,000 km yet averages only about 10 meters thick.

entries.title: Uranus
entries.blurb: An ice giant tipped on its side — its axis lies almost in its orbital plane, giving 42-year-long polar seasons.

entries.title: Neptune
entries.blurb: The most distant planet, an ice giant with the fastest winds measured in the Solar System — up to ~2,100 km/h.

entries.title: Pluto
entries.blurb: The best-known dwarf planet: New Horizons revealed nitrogen-ice glaciers and the heart-shaped Sputnik Planitia.

entries.title: The Sun

photo.file: The Sun by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly of NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory - 20100819.jpg

entries.blurb: Our star: a 4.6-billion-year-old G-type dwarf converting 600 million tonnes of hydrogen to helium every second, 150 million km away.
entries.source: T_eff 5772 K: IAU nominal solar values, Prša et al. 2016

entries.title: The Moon
entries.blurb: Earth's only natural satellite, 384,400 km away on average — the only world beyond Earth that humans have walked on.
entries.source: Mean distance: standard lunar ephemeris value

entries.title: Sagittarius A*
entries.blurb: The first direct image of the Milky Way's own supermassive black hole, released by the Event Horizon Telescope in May 2022.

entries.title: M87*
entries.blurb: The first photograph of a black hole ever taken — the Event Horizon Telescope's 2019 image of the 6.5-billion-solar-mass giant at the heart of M87.

entries.title: Betelgeuse
entries.blurb: A red supergiant near the end of its life, ~550 light-years away — one of very few stars whose surface we can actually resolve. When it explodes as a supernova it will briefly outshine the full Moon.
entries.source: T_eff ~3600 K: Levesque et al. 2005, ApJ 628, 973

entries.title: Sirius
entries.blurb: The brightest star in the night sky — a hot white A-type star 8.6 light-years away, orbited by a white-dwarf companion.

entries.title: Vega
entries.blurb: The historical zero-point of the magnitude scale and a former (and future) pole star, 25 light-years away.

entries.title: Rigel
entries.blurb: A blue supergiant roughly 120,000 times as luminous as the Sun, marking Orion's western foot.
entries.source: T_eff ~12,100 K: Przybilla et al. 2006, A&A 445, 1099

entries.title: Antares
entries.blurb: The 'rival of Mars' — a red supergiant so large that placed at the Sun's position it would engulf the orbit of Mars.
entries.source: T_eff ~3660 K: Ohnaka et al. 2013, A&A 555, A24

entries.title: Polaris
entries.blurb: The current North Star — actually a Cepheid variable supergiant in a triple system, ~430 light-years away.
entries.source: T_eff ~6015 K: Usenko et al. 2005; distance approx., parallax debated

entries.title: Proxima Centauri
entries.blurb: The nearest star to the Sun at 4.24 light-years — a dim red dwarf prone to violent flares, hosting at least one planet.
entries.source: T_eff ~3042 K: Ségransan et al. 2003, A&A 397, L5

entries.title: Crab Nebula

photo.credit: NASA/ESA, J. Hester & A. Loll (Arizona State University)

entries.blurb: The expanding wreckage of a supernova witnessed worldwide in 1054 CE, powered by a neutron star spinning 30 times a second at its heart.

entries.title: Andromeda Galaxy
entries.blurb: Our nearest large galactic neighbor, 2.5 million light-years away and on a slow collision course with the Milky Way.

entries.title: Orion Nebula

photo.credit: NASA/ESA, M. Robberto (STScI) & Hubble Orion Treasury Team

entries.blurb: The nearest massive star-forming region to Earth, 1,344 light-years away — a stellar nursery visible to the naked eye.

entries.title: Whirlpool Galaxy

photo.credit: NASA/ESA, S. Beckwith (STScI) & Hubble Heritage Team

entries.blurb: A textbook grand-design spiral, its arms sharpened by an ongoing encounter with the companion galaxy NGC 5195.

entries.title: Eagle Nebula — Pillars of Creation

photo.file: Pillars of creation 2014 HST WFC3-UVIS full-res.jpg

entries.blurb: Towering columns of cold gas and dust sculpted by radiation from nearby newborn stars — Hubble's most famous image, re-shot in 2014.

entries.title: 51 Pegasi b

photo.file: Artist impression of the exoplanet 51 Pegasi b.jpg

entries.blurb: The first planet ever found orbiting a Sun-like star (1995) — a 'hot Jupiter' racing around its star every 4.2 days. Its discovery earned the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.

entries.title: HD 189733 b
entries.blurb: A hot Jupiter whose deep cobalt-blue color was actually measured with Hubble — likely molten silicate glass raining sideways in ~8,700 km/h winds.
entries.source: Blue albedo: Evans et al. 2013, ApJL 772, L16

entries.title: HD 209458 b
entries.blurb: 'Osiris' — the first exoplanet observed transiting its star and the first with a detected atmosphere, which is slowly evaporating into space.
entries.source: Charbonneau et al. 2000, ApJL 529, L45; Vidal-Madjar et al. 2003, Nature 422, 143

entries.title: 55 Cancri e
entries.blurb: A super-Earth so close to its star that its year lasts 18 hours and its dayside is likely an ocean of molten rock.
entries.source: Dayside T ~2700 K: Demory et al. 2016, Nature 532, 207

entries.title: TRAPPIST-1 e
entries.blurb: One of seven Earth-sized worlds packed around the ultracool dwarf TRAPPIST-1 — and among the most promising temperate rocky planets known.
entries.source: Gillon et al. 2017, Nature 542, 456; surface appearance unknown, render illustrative

entries.title: Proxima Centauri b

photo.file: Artist’s impression of Proxima Centauri b.jpg

entries.blurb: The closest known exoplanet — a roughly Earth-mass world in the habitable zone of the star nearest to the Sun.

entries.title: Kepler-452 b
entries.blurb: Nicknamed 'Earth's older cousin': a super-Earth in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star about 1.5 billion years older than ours.

entries.title: Kepler-186 f
entries.blurb: The first Earth-sized planet found in another star's habitable zone, orbiting a cool red dwarf 580 light-years away.
entries.source: Quintana et al. 2014, Science 344, 277; surface appearance unknown, render illustrative

entries.title: GJ 1214 b
entries.blurb: A hazy sub-Neptune 'water world' whose featureless, cloud-shrouded spectrum frustrated a decade of atmosphere studies.

entries.title: WASP-12 b
entries.blurb: An ultra-hot Jupiter darker than fresh asphalt, so close to its star that it is being stretched into an egg shape and devoured.
entries.source: Albedo: Bell et al. 2017, ApJL 847, L2; tidal distortion: Li et al. 2010, Nature 463, 1054

entries.title: Kepler-16 b
entries.blurb: The 'Tatooine' planet — a cold Saturn-mass world that orbits two suns at once, the first unambiguous circumbinary planet.

entries.title: TRAPPIST-1 e
entries.blurb: One of seven Earth-sized worlds packed around an ultracool red dwarf 40 light-years away — the richest known system of rocky, potentially temperate planets.

entries.title: Kepler-22 b
entries.blurb: The first confirmed planet found in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star (2011).

entries.title: 55 Cancri e
entries.blurb: A lava world twice Earth's size racing around its star every 18 hours — its dayside is an ocean of molten rock.

entries.title: K2-18 b
entries.blurb: A temperate sub-Neptune where Hubble found water vapour in the atmosphere (2019) — and JWST later found carbon-bearing molecules.
entries._photo_note: Former Commons artist-impression filename 404s (caught by the daily health check, 2026-07-11); procedural render until a verified filename replaces it.

entries.title: WASP-12 b
entries.blurb: One of the darkest and hottest planets known — pulled egg-shaped by tides and being devoured by its star.
entries._photo_note: Former Commons artist-impression filename 404s (caught by the daily health check, 2026-07-11); procedural render until a verified filename replaces it.

entries.title: GJ 1214 b
entries.blurb: The archetypal 'water world' candidate — a steamy sub-Neptune whose deep atmosphere may blanket a global ocean.

entries.title: HR 8799 system
entries.blurb: The first multi-planet system ever directly imaged — four super-Jupiters, photographed often enough that we can watch them actually orbit.

photo.credit: Jason Wang (Northwestern)/Christian Marois (NRC-HIA), W. M. Keck Observatory

entries.title: 2M1207 b
entries.blurb: The first exoplanet ever photographed (VLT, 2004) — a young, glowing super-Jupiter beside a brown dwarf.

entries.title: Fomalhaut b (Dagon)
entries.blurb: Imaged by Hubble inside Fomalhaut's great dust ring; later studies suggest it may be an expanding cloud from a colossal planetesimal collision rather than a planet.

photo.file: Fomalhaut with Disk Ring and extrasolar planet b.jpg

entries.title: Beta Pictoris b
entries.blurb: A young super-Jupiter directly imaged crossing the famous debris disk of Beta Pictoris.

entries.title: PDS 70 b
entries.blurb: A planet caught in the act of forming — directly imaged still embedded in the disk of gas and dust it is being born from.

entries.title: TOI-700 d
entries.blurb: TESS's first Earth-sized planet in a habitable zone, 100 light-years away.

entries.title: Ring Nebula

photo.file: Hubble reveals the Ring Nebula’s true shape.jpg

entries.blurb: A dying Sun-like star's cast-off atmosphere glowing as a luminous ring 2,000 light-years away — a preview of our own Sun's fate.

entries.title: Helix Nebula
entries.blurb: One of the nearest planetary nebulae — the 'Eye of God' — a dying star's shells of gas seen almost pole-on, 650 light-years away.

entries.title: Sombrero Galaxy
entries.blurb: A nearly edge-on spiral with a brilliant bulge and a dramatic dust lane brim, home to a billion-solar-mass central black hole.

entries.title: Pleiades
entries.blurb: The Seven Sisters: a young star cluster drifting through a chance dust cloud that scatters their blue light into wispy veils.

entries.title: Lagoon Nebula
entries.blurb: A giant stellar nursery in Sagittarius, visible to the naked eye — glowing hydrogen carved by winds from its newborn stars.

entries.title: Trifid Nebula
entries.blurb: Three nebulae in one: pink emission, blue reflection, and the dark dust lanes that split it into three lobes and give it its name.

entries.title: Omega Nebula
entries.blurb: One of the Milky Way's most active star factories, its glowing checkmark of gas lit by a hidden cluster of young massive stars.

entries.title: Dumbbell Nebula
entries.blurb: The first planetary nebula ever discovered (1764) — twin lobes of gas shed by a dying star, 1,360 light-years away in Vulpecula.

entries.title: Cat's Eye Nebula

photo.file: Cat's Eye Nebula - NGC 6543 - NASA ESA Hubble Space Telescope (52479198918).png

entries.blurb: One of the most intricate planetary nebulae known — eleven concentric shells, jets and knots around a dying star in Draco.

entries.title: Eskimo Nebula
entries.blurb: A dying star wrapped in a 'parka' of comet-shaped filaments — the inner face is gas blown outward in the last 10,000 years.

entries.title: Horsehead Nebula
entries.blurb: The sky's most famous dark nebula: a horse-head pillar of cold dust silhouetted against glowing hydrogen in Orion's Belt.

entries.title: Carina Nebula
entries.blurb: A southern star-forming giant four times larger than Orion, home to the unstable supergiant Eta Carinae — a supernova in waiting.

entries.title: Veil Nebula
entries.blurb: Delicate glowing filaments — the shredded remains of a star that exploded some 10–20,000 years ago, still expanding across Cygnus.

entries.title: Rosette Nebula
entries.blurb: A vast cosmic rose in Monoceros: the young cluster NGC 2244 has hollowed out the heart of the cloud that formed it.

entries.title: North America Nebula

photo.file: NGC 7000- The North America Nebula and the Pelican Nebula (noao-n7000mosblock).jpg

entries.blurb: An emission cloud shaped uncannily like a continent, beside its companion the Pelican — both lit by hidden hot young stars in Cygnus.

entries.title: Tarantula Nebula
entries.blurb: The most violent star-forming region in the Local Group, in the Large Magellanic Cloud — if it sat where Orion is, it would cast shadows.

entries.title: Triangulum Galaxy

photo.credit: NASA/ESA Hubble (M. Durbin, J. Dalcanton, B.F. Williams)

entries.blurb: The third-largest galaxy of our Local Group, a floculent spiral seen nearly face-on — Hubble resolved 25 million of its stars.

entries.title: Pinwheel Galaxy
entries.blurb: A grand face-on spiral nearly twice the Milky Way's diameter — this Hubble portrait was stitched from ten years of exposures.

entries.title: Butterfly Nebula
entries.blurb: Wings of gas hotter than 20,000 °C torn from one of the hottest dying stars known — 250,000 °C at the nebula's hidden heart.

entries.title: Bubble Nebula
entries.blurb: A seven-light-year soap bubble blown by the ferocious wind of a star 45 times the Sun's mass — Hubble's 26th anniversary image.

entries.title: Centaurus A
entries.blurb: The nearest active galaxy: an elliptical that swallowed a spiral, its central black hole firing jets seen here in submillimetre and X-ray light.

entries.title: Antennae Galaxies
entries.blurb: Two spirals caught mid-collision, igniting billions of new stars — a preview of the Milky Way's eventual merger with Andromeda.

entries.title: Omega Centauri

photo.file: VST image of the giant globular star cluster Omega Centauri.jpg

entries.blurb: The Milky Way's largest globular cluster — ten million stars, possibly the stripped core of a dwarf galaxy we absorbed long ago.

entries.title: 47 Tucanae

photo.credit: ESO/M.-R. Cioni/VISTA Magellanic Cloud survey, CC BY 4.0

entries.blurb: The southern sky's second-brightest globular cluster: up to a million ancient stars packed into a ball 120 light-years across.

entries.title: Great Hercules Cluster
entries.blurb: The northern sky's showpiece globular — several hundred thousand stars, target of the 1974 Arecibo message to any listeners there.

entries.title: Bode's Galaxy
entries.blurb: A textbook grand-design spiral 12 million light-years away, locked in a gravitational tug-of-war with its neighbor the Cigar Galaxy.

entries.title: Cigar Galaxy
entries.blurb: A starburst galaxy forming stars ten times faster than the Milky Way, venting towers of glowing hydrogen from its core.

entries.title: Southern Pinwheel Galaxy
entries.blurb: A barred spiral rich in supernovae — six observed in the last century, more than almost any other galaxy.

entries.title: Black Eye Galaxy

photo.credit: NASA and the Hubble Heritage Team (AURA/STScI)

entries.blurb: A smouldering dark dust band across a bright core — and gas in its outskirts orbiting backwards, relic of an ancient merger.

entries.title: Sculptor Galaxy
entries.blurb: The dusty 'Silver Coin' — one of the brightest galaxies beyond the Local Group and a furious hidden starburst behind its dust.

entries.title: Stephan's Quintet
entries.blurb: A visual grouping of five galaxies, four locked in a slow gravitational dance of collisions and tidal tails.

entries.title: Cartwheel Galaxy
entries.blurb: A bullseye 500 million light-years away: a smaller galaxy punched straight through a spiral, sending a ring of starbirth rippling outward.

entries.title: Flame Nebula

photo.file: The hidden fires of the Flame Nebula.jpg

entries.blurb: Alnitak's ultraviolet glare sets this Orion cloud alight; in infrared, VISTA sees straight through the dark dust lane that splits it.
